questions.problem: Determine the entry ${a}_{12}^{′}$ in the inverse of a matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A)=|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}| & =1|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|-(-2)|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}|+4|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(6-0)+2(0+1)+4(0+3) \\  & =6+2+12 \\  & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since we want the entry ${a}_{12}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{21}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{21} & =(-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(-4-0) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{12}^{′}=\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{21}=\frac{1}{20}\cdot 4=\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Determine the entry ${a}_{31}^{′}$ in the inverse of a matrix $A$ $=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the determinant of $A:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}A=|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}| & =(-1)|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}|-1|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}|+0|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(2+1)-(1-2)+0 \\  & =-3+1+0 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since we want the entry ${a}_{31}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{13}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{13} & =(-1)^{1+3}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-1-4 \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{31}^{′}=\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{13}=\frac{1}{-2}\cdot (-5)=\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The entry ${a}_{22}^{′}$ in the inverse of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & k & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]$
equals $-\frac{1}{4}$ and $det(A)=k-4.$ Find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, note that we are given the determinant of $A:$

$$
det(A)=k-4
$$

Since we want the entry ${a}_{22}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{22}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{22} & =(-1)^{2+2}|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1-0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{22}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{22} \\  & =\frac{1}{k-4}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{k-4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are told that ${a}_{22}^{′}=-\frac{1}{4}$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{k-4} \\ k-4 & =-4 \\ k & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Determine the entry ${a}_{31}^{′}$ in the inverse of a matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].$

${a}_{31}^{′}=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A)=|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}| & =1|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}|-0|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|+2|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\,(2+1)-0\,(0-1)+2\,(-0-2) \\  & =3-0-4 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since we want the entry ${a}_{31}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{31}^{t}={c}_{13}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{13} & =(-1)^{1+3}|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =+|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-0 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{31}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{31}^{t} \\  & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{13} \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}\cdot (-2) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The entry ${a}_{12}^{′}$ in the inverse of the matrix

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ k & -1 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

equals $-\frac{1}{2}.$ Find the value of $k.$

$k=${{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ k & -1 & 2\end{aligned}|=1|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}|-2|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ k & 2\end{aligned}|+(-1)|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ k & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\,(1\cdot 2-1\cdot (-1))-2\,(0\cdot 2-1\cdot k)+(-1)\,(0\cdot (-1)-1\cdot k) \\  & =(2+1)-2\,(-k)+(-1)\,(-k) \\  & =3+2k+k \\  & =3k+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want the entry ${a}_{12}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need ${c}_{12}^{t}={c}_{21}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{21} & =(-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(2\cdot 2-(-1)\cdot (-1)) \\  & =-(4-1) \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{12}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{12}^{t} \\  & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{21} \\  & =\frac{1}{3k+3}\cdot (-3) \\  & =\frac{-3}{3k+3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we are told that ${a}_{12}^{′}=-\frac{1}{2}$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-3}{3k+3} & =-\frac{1}{2} \\ -3k-3 & =-6 \\ -3k & =-6+3 \\ k & =\frac{-3}{-3} \\ k & =1.\end{aligned}
$$
